entry: Thermodynamic potential, symbol *G*, measuring the maximum work, other than pressure–volume work, that a closed system can perform at constant temperature and pressure. It is defined as G = H − TS, where H is [[Enthalpy]] and S is [[Entropy]]. This maximum is attained only in a completely reversible process. A reduction in G is necessary for a reaction to be spontaneous under these conditions, and G is minimized when a system reaches [[Chemical equilibrium|chemical equilibrium]]. The concept, originally called "available energy," was developed in the 1870s by [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]].

British Overseas Territory and city near the southern tip of the [[Iberian Peninsula]], at the western entrance of the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. The Rock of Gibraltar dominates the landscape, and around 38,000 people, primarily Gibraltarians, live at its foot. The Almohads founded a permanent watchtower there in 1160. Anglo-Dutch forces captured it from Spain in 1704 during the [[War of the Spanish Succession]], and it was ceded to Great Britain in perpetuity by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713. Controlling the [[Strait of Gibraltar]], it became an important base for the [[Royal Navy]], particularly in the Napoleonic Wars and [[World War II]]. Spain asserts a claim to the territory, but Gibraltarians overwhelmingly rejected Spanish sovereignty in a 1967 referendum and shared sovereignty in 2002. Since [[Brexit]], Gibraltar has been outside the [[European Union]]. Its economy rests on online gambling, financial services, tourism and the port.

Genus of large carcharodontosaurid theropod dinosaur from Cretaceous [[Argentina]]. Its holotype, almost 70% complete, was found in the Candeleros Formation of Patagonia in 1993 and named *Giganotosaurus carolinii* in 1995 after its discoverer, Rubén Carolini. Estimates for the most complete specimen give a length of 12 to 13 m and a weight of 4.2 to 13.8 t, and some researchers consider it larger than [[Tyrannosaurus]], while others find the two roughly equal. It is thought to have been the [[Apex predator]] of its ecosystem, possibly feeding on juvenile sauropod dinosaurs.

Extinct genus of great [[Ape|ape]] from central and southern China, represented by one species, *Gigantopithecus blacki*. Known only from teeth and four mandibles, it was first identified in 1935 from two third-molar teeth in a [[Hong Kong]] drugstore. Once argued to be a hominin, it is now thought to be closely allied with [[Orangutan|orangutans]] and may have weighed 200–300 kilograms. A generalist herbivore, it probably became extinct about 300,000 years ago, possibly through habitat loss from climate change and archaic human activity. In cryptozoology it is popularly identified with the [[Yeti|yeti]] and the American [[Bigfoot|bigfoot]].

Venomous lizard and the largest species native to the United States. Its scientific name is *Heloderma suspectum*, and it is a heavy, slow-moving [[Reptile|reptile]] up to 22 in (56 cm) long. It lives in the deserts of [[Arizona]], [[New Mexico]], [[California]], [[Nevada]] and [[Utah]] and northwestern [[Mexico]]. It is the only venomous lizard native to the United States, but though its bite is painful, it very rarely poses a real threat to humans. Its lower teeth have venom grooves, and it is protected by state law in Arizona, though it is sometimes killed. One of its venom peptides, exendin-4, formed the basis for GLP-1 receptor agonists used to treat type 2 diabetes and [[Obesity|obesity]].

American physical chemist and dean of the college of chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. Best known for his discovery of the [[Covalent bond|covalent bond]] and his concept of electron pairs, Lewis devised electron-dot structures and contributed to [[Valence bond theory|valence bond theory]], which shaped modern understanding of chemical bonding. In 1916 he proposed his theory of bonding and added electron information to the periodic table. He also advanced chemical thermodynamics and [[Photochemistry|photochemistry]], and he is known for his concept of [[Acid|acids]] and bases. In 1926 he coined the term *photon* for the smallest unit of radiant energy. From 1933 he researched isotope separation and purified a sample of [[Heavy water]]. He was nominated 41 times for the [[Nobel Prize]] in Chemistry but never won it. He moved to Berkeley in 1912 and mentored Nobel laureates there, including [[Harold Urey]].

Victorian-era theatrical partnership of the dramatist W. S. Gilbert and composer Arthur Sullivan. The two collaborated on fourteen comic operas between 1871 and 1896, of which *H.M.S. Pinafore*, *The Pirates of Penzance* and *The Mikado* are among the best known. The producer Richard D'Oyly Carte brought them together, built the Savoy Theatre in 1881 for their works, and founded the D'Oyly Carte Opera Company, which performed them for more than a century. Gilbert's witty, satiric libretti created topsy-turvy worlds in which each absurdity is taken to its logical conclusion, while Sullivan's memorable melodies conveyed both humor and pathos. Their operas influenced [[Musical theatre|musical theatre]] through the 20th century and have been widely parodied.

American actress and comedian. One of the seven original cast members of *Saturday Night Live* from 1975 to 1980, she won an Emmy Award in 1978. She later appeared in films with her husband, [[Gene Wilder]]. Diagnosed with ovarian [[Cancer|cancer]] in 1986, she published her autobiography, *It's Always Something*, shortly before her death. Her widower helped found organizations promoting early diagnosis and support for cancer patients, as she had wished. Posthumously she won a Grammy Award in 1990 and received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2003.

Period of United States history from the late 1870s to the late 1890s, between Reconstruction and the [[Progressive Era]]. Named after [[Mark Twain]]'s 1873 novel *The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today*, it was a time of rapid economic growth, especially in the North and West. Real wages rose 40% from 1860 to 1890, yet visible poverty persisted, and urban [[Slum|slums]] grew alongside a concentration of wealth. Powerful trusts formed, some effectively creating monopolies, and African Americans in the South lost political power and voting rights after Reconstruction ended in 1877.

Respiratory organ in many aquatic animals, extracting dissolved [[Oxygen|oxygen]] from water and excreting [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Gills occur in [[Crustacean|crustaceans]], molluscs, xiphosurans, aquatic insects, polychaetes and most aquatic [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]], including [[Fish|fish]] and amphibian tadpoles. Their filaments and *lamellae* (folds) present a large surface area, and blood or body fluid within them exchanges gases through thin walls before the [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]] distributes them. This surface area matters because water holds only a small fraction of the oxygen in air and diffuses it more slowly. Semi-terrestrial animals such as [[Crab|crabs]] and mudskippers store water in gill chambers to survive on land. In [[Spider|spiders]] and scorpions, ancestral gills evolved into air-breathing book lungs.

American actress and writer. She is best known for playing FBI agent Dana Scully in *The X-Files*, a role that won her a Primetime Emmy Award and was revived in a series from 2016 to 2018. She played British Prime Minister [[Margaret Thatcher]] in the fourth season of *The Crown*, earning a second Golden Globe and Primetime Emmy Award. On stage she won the Evening Standard Theatre Award for Best Actress for playing Blanche DuBois in *A Streetcar Named Desire*. In 2016 she was appointed an honorary Officer of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (OBE) for services to drama.

American [[Sitcom|sitcom]] created by Sherwood Schwartz and broadcast on [[CBS]]. Seven castaways are shipwrecked on an uncharted Pacific island after a storm on a three-hour tour from [[Honolulu]]. Most episodes turn on conflicts among the castaways and their attempts to escape, and their rescue attempts are typically thwarted by the inept first mate, Gilligan. The show ran for 98 episodes over three seasons, from September 26, 1964, to April 17, 1967. The first season was filmed in black and white, and the second and third in color. Its popularity grew in syndication, especially in the 1970s and 1980s.

Flowering plant, *Zingiber officinale*, prized for its rhizome as a spice and folk medicine. An herbaceous perennial in the family Zingiberaceae, which includes [[Turmeric|turmeric]] and [[Cardamom|cardamom]], it grows pseudostems about one meter tall. Ginger originated in Maritime Southeast Asia and was first domesticated by the [[Austronesian peoples]], who carried it across the Indo-Pacific as far as Hawaii. It was one of the first spices exported from Asia, reaching Europe with the spice trade and used by ancient Greeks and Romans. It has long been used in traditional medicine in China, India and Japan. Ginger may offer benefits over placebo for nausea and vomiting during pregnancy, but it remains uncertain whether it is effective for treating any disease. In 2023, world production was 4.9 million [[Tonne|tonnes]], led by India with 45% of the total.

American actress, dancer and singer of Hollywood's Golden Age. Born in Independence, Missouri, she moved with her family to [[Fort Worth, Texas|Fort Worth]] as a child. In 1925 she won a Charleston contest that helped launch a [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] career, and her Broadway debut in *Girl Crazy* led to a contract with [[Paramount Pictures]]. Supporting roles in *42nd Street* and *Gold Diggers of 1933* were her first successful films. Her RKO musicals with [[Fred Astaire]], including *Top Hat* (1935) and *Swing Time* (1936), are credited with revolutionizing the genre. She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Kitty Foyle* (1940) and made 73 films in her career. She returned to Broadway in *Hello, Dolly!* in 1965, and in 1992 was honored at the Kennedy Center Honors.

Measure of statistical dispersion representing income or wealth inequality within a nation or [[Social group|social group]]. Italian statistician Corrado Gini published it in 1912. It ranges from 0, indicating perfect equality, to 1 (or 100%), indicating maximal inequality. For [[OECD]] countries in the late 20th century, after taxes and transfers, the income Gini ranged from 0.24 to 0.49, with [[Slovakia]] lowest and [[Mexico]] highest. In 2008–2009, [[South Africa]] had the world's highest pre-tax coefficient, estimated at 0.63 to 0.7. Because many distribution curves can yield the same value, interpretation requires care.

Species of gymnosperm tree native to [[East Asia]], also known as the maidenhair tree. It is the last living species in the order Ginkgoales, which first appeared over 290 million years ago, and fossils similar to it date back to the Middle [[Jurassic]], about 170 million years ago. Widely regarded as a [[Fossil|living fossil]], it is long-lived: specimens have been measured at more than 1,600 years, and the largest living trees are estimated to exceed 3,500 years. Its fan-shaped leaves turn yellow in autumn, and its seeds resemble [[Apricot|apricots]] but are not true fruits. Widely planted in [[City|cities]] for its pollution tolerance, some trees survived the atomic bombing of [[Hiroshima]]. Ginkgo-based products are marketed for cognitive benefits, but clinical research shows limited effectiveness except possibly for [[Dementia|dementia]].

Root of plants in the genus *Panax*, used in herbal preparations. Species include Korean ginseng (*Panax ginseng*), South China ginseng (*Panax notoginseng*) and American ginseng (*Panax quinquefolius*), whose roots contain ginsenosides and gintonin. Ginseng has long been used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]] in Korea and China, but there is no substantial evidence that it treats any medical condition, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has not approved it to prevent or treat disease. [[Dietary supplement|Supplements]] have sometimes been contaminated with unrelated filler compounds, and excessive use may interact with [[Prescription drug|prescription drugs]]. Wild American ginseng can be harvested in 19 states and the [[Appalachian Mountains]], but its export is restricted, and wild ginseng is almost extinct in China and endangered globally.

Italian composer and conductor of the late Classical and early Romantic eras, known for opera. Born in Pesaro, then part of the [[Papal States]], to musician parents, he began composing by age twelve and studied in [[Bologna]]. He wrote 39 operas, including the comic *Il barbiere di Siviglia* and *La Cenerentola* and the serious *Tancredi*, *Otello* and *Semiramide*, and between 1810 and 1823 he wrote 34 operas for Italian stages. In 1815 he was engaged to manage theatres in [[Naples]]. In 1824 he was contracted by the Opéra in Paris, and his last opera, *Guillaume Tell*, appeared in 1829. His withdrawal from opera for the last 40 years of his life has never been fully explained. In Paris after 1855 he hosted musical salons attended by [[Franz Liszt]] and [[Giuseppe Verdi]].

Italian philosopher, Dominican friar and cosmological theorist. Born Filippo Bruno in Nola, near [[Naples]], he entered the Dominican order, was ordained a priest, and wrote extensively on the art of memory and on cosmology. He proposed that stars are distant suns with their own [[Exoplanet|exoplanets]], possibly with life of their own, and that the universe is infinite and has no centre. The Roman [[Inquisition]] tried him for [[Heresy|heresy]], including denial of the [[Trinity]] and transubstantiation, and his [[Pantheism|pantheism]] also drew condemnation. He refused to recant and was burned at the stake in Rome's Campo de' Fiori. Some historians believe the trial responded more to his religious views than to his cosmology, while others reject this view, and his case remains a landmark in the history of free thought.

Italian politician and Prime Minister of Italy since October 2022. She is the first woman to hold the office and leads the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian Republic. She co-founded Brothers of Italy (FdI) in 2012 and has led it since 2014. A [[Conservatism|conservative]] and right-wing populist who opposes euthanasia and same-sex marriage, she supports [[NATO]] while holding Eurosceptic views of the [[European Union]]. Some critics describe her as xenophobic and Islamophobic.

Italian Renaissance painter, architect, art historian and biographer. His *Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects* is considered the ideological foundation of Western art-historical writing, though it contains many factual errors, especially about artists who lived before his birth. Effectively the minister of culture to the Medici court in [[Florence]], he helped found the Florentine Accademia in 1563 and designed the tomb of his hero [[Michelangelo]] in Santa Croce. Vasari's account of [[Giotto]]'s new manner of painting as a rebirth led the French historian Jules Michelet to adopt the term [[Renaissance]] in 1835.

Italian painter and architect from [[Florence]] during the Late Middle Ages. His masterwork is the fresco cycle in the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua, completed around 1305, which depicts the Life of the Virgin and the Life of Christ and is regarded as one of the supreme masterpieces of the Early Renaissance. In 1334 the Commune of Florence chose him to design the new campanile of the [[Florence Cathedral]]. [[Giorgio Vasari|Vasari]] credited him with breaking decisively from the Byzantine style and initiating the great art of painting as we know it today, but many aspects of his life are uncertain, including his birthplace, apprenticeship and burial. Pupils such as Taddeo Gaddi and later masters including [[Masaccio]] emulated his innovations in light, anatomy and narrative drama.

Italian writer, poet and Renaissance humanist, correspondent of [[Petrarch]]. His best-known work, *The Decameron*, is a collection of short stories told by ten young Florentines who flee the [[Black Death]] to a villa. Its realistic dialogue differed from medieval formulas, and after Pietro Bembo elevated its style into a model of Italian prose in the sixteenth century, it influenced [[Geoffrey Chaucer]], [[Miguel de Cervantes]] and [[Lope de Vega]]. Boccaccio is one of the Three Crowns of Italian literature, with [[Dante Alighieri|Dante]] and Petrarch. He copied codices of the *Divine Comedy* and promoted Dante's work through public lectures, and with Petrarch he helped lay the foundations of humanism in Florence.

Italian composer of late Renaissance music and central figure of the Roman School. Born in Palestrina in the [[Papal States]], he moved to [[Rome]] as a child. In 1551 Pope Julius III appointed him maestro di cappella of the Cappella Giulia at [[St. Peter's Basilica]], but he had to leave four years later because, as a married man, he could not continue as a layman under Pope Paul IV. He returned in 1571 and remained at St Peter's until his death. His masses, numbering over 105, and his motets exerted influence, but the so-called Palestrinian style of [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]], as codified by Johann Joseph Fux, had the greatest influence. According to Grove Music Online, his success in reconciling the aims of Catholic church music after the Council of Trent earned him an enduring reputation as the ideal Catholic composer.

Large African hoofed mammal, the tallest living terrestrial animal and largest [[Ruminant|ruminant]]. Giraffes have extremely long necks and legs, horn-like ossicones and spotted coats. Their range extends from [[Chad]] to [[South Africa]], where they inhabit [[Savanna|savannahs]] and woodlands and browse leaves and fruits of woody plants, mainly acacias, at heights most other ground-based [[Herbivore|herbivores]] cannot reach. Males establish dominance by "necking," fighting with their necks, and dominant males gain mating access to females, which alone rear the young. Traditionally treated as one species, *Giraffa camelopardalis*, with nine subspecies, giraffes have more recently been proposed to comprise four species. Estimates as of 2016 put the wild population at about 97,500.
